sources.citation: Walker 1982, A Grammar of Sawu, NUSA 13, sec. 2.6 Word stress (pp. 7-8), full PDF re-read from sealang.net/archives/nusa/pdf/
sources.quote: As the majority of Sawu words have stress on the penultimate syllable, I prefer to analyze stressed consonant plus long vowel (i.e. (CV:) as disyllabic 'CVV with predictable penultimate stress. ... Words of four-or-more syllables are stressed on every second syllable from the end. e.g wo'pəka'lae 'ankle'.

sources.citation: Pappas, Leah. 2022. A Multi-Modal Study of Spatial Language in Hawu in Typological Perspective. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. 280 pp. (ScholarSpace)
sources.quote: 'I only offer very preliminary observations, and notably, my assumption that there even is word-level stress should be questioned. Hawu appears to have fixed word-level stress on the penultimate syllable, regardless of how many syllables are in the word. Stress is indicated by a slightly higher pitch and intensity which is very consistently on the penultimate vowel. Vowel length does not indicate stress ... even long vowels do not appear to attract stress. ... Even penultimate schwa ... has a higher pitch and intensity than the ultimate-syllable vowel.' Confirms penult primary; silent on Walke
sources.note: Most recent fieldwork-based sketch (ch. 5) with a stress subsection (p. 107) giving impressionistic pitch/intensity cues on the penult and an explicit caution that word-level stress is unverified — worth citing as the modern confirmation and caveat.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. 2010. Hawu and Dhao in eastern Indonesia: revisiting their relationship. In Michael Ewing & Marian Klamer (eds), East Nusantara: typological and areal analyses (Pacific Linguistics 618), 251-280. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.quote: 'Phonetically long vowels are a sequence of two vowels. There are no single unit diphthongs. Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Each vowel is a syllable nucleus, so stress falls on the penultimate vowel in VV sequences, regardless of whether the two vowels are the same or different. A stressed schwa /ə/ in a VCV# sequence results in phonetic lengthening of the following consonant.' and 'The six-vowel systems and word stress are virtually identical between the two languages [Hawu, Dhao].' Silent on secondary/rhythmic stress.
sources.note: Independent post-Walker first-hand phonology section by the SIL/UBB linguist who worked on Hawu; p. 259 confirms penultimate stress and VV = two syllables — second source for the record's refs.
sources.venue: East Nusantara: typological and areal analyses (Pacific Linguistics 618)

sources.citation: Walker, Alan T. 1982. A Grammar of Sawu (NUSA 13). Jakarta: Badan Penyelenggara Seri NUSA, Universitas Atma Jaya. xv+75 pp. [sealang image-only scan + ANU Open Research copy with text, hdl 1885/111434]
sources.quote: 'As the majority of Sawu words have stress on the penultimate syllable, I prefer to analyze stressed consonant plus long vowel (i.e. (CV:) as disyllabic 'CVV with predictable penultimate stress. ... This analysis highlights Sawu's clear preference for penultimate stress ... Words of four-or-more syllables are stressed on every second syllable from the end. e.g wo'peka'lae.' p. 3: 'We agree [with Radja Haba 1958] that word stress falls on the penultimate syllable'.

tone.quote: There are no tautosyllabic consonant clusters. Hawu has many words of the shape (C)Vx.Vy, these sequences are disyllabic (Grimes 2006). Long vowels cannot be found preceding a consonant: *CVVCV(CV). If they do occur (they appear to be final: [niŋa:] 'what' and maybe ideophonic, even so, long vowels are always disyllabic (Grimes 2006). Stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable (Walker 1982). The only vowel in the antepenultimate syllable is 'e'. The canonical word-shape is: (C)(e)(C)V(C)V (Blust 2008:7).
tone.locator: lingbuzz preprint p. 2, sec. 1 'Hawu basics' (end of consonant inventory, before 1.1 'Vowel quality and its position in the word')
